artboards.title: The Releases view (A and B share it)
Option C — Plan, with the record as a rail

annotations.text:
The question

Phases and releases are orthogonal. A phase is a unit of PLAN — named ahead of time, holds tasks, has progress. A release is a unit of RECORD — a version that went out on a date, holds no tasks.

Stacking them on one page implies a relationship neither has to the other. Each option below answers "so where do releases live" differently.

One thing is shared by all four, so it isn't what you're choosing between: the phase list is grouped by state, and finished phases collapse to one line. That's what kills the wall of summary text.

Option A — Two tabs

Your suggestion. One nav slot, one thing on screen at a time.

For: the cheapest change, and the tab bar states outright that these are two lists rather than one.
Against: a tab is a place things hide. Releases become invisible unless you remember to look, and you can't see the plan and the record together.

Option B — Two screens

Releases gets its own rail entry and its own keyboard number. Roadmap means phases, full stop.

For: the honest structure — two nouns, two screens — and each gets a title that says what it is.
Against: a tenth nav item for ten rows that change once a week. The rail is the app's scarcest space.

Option C — Plan, with the record as a rail

Both on one screen, but shaped so differently that nobody would read them as one list. The rail is the only thing here with real dates.

For: you see what shipped while looking at what's planned, which is the question a Sunday review actually asks.
Against: 300px off the phase column, and it still puts two nouns on one screen — the thing you flagged.

Option D — Demote, don't move

The argument against your diagnosis, included so the vote isn't rigged. Maybe adjacency was never the problem — maybe it was that ten release rows got full card treatment they don't deserve.

For: no new tab, no new screen, one scroll answers both questions.
Against: if you're right that these are orthogonal, this leaves them adjacent and just makes one of them quieter.
